sentences.text: Carcharodontosaurus saharicus grew to about 12 meters in length and weighed between 5 and 7 metric tons, making it one of the largest known theropods.
The complete neotype skull of this species would measure 1.6 meters, a size comparable to the largest skulls of Tyrannosaurus.
It was a robust theropod characterized by small forelimbs, an elongated tail, and a short neck.
The animal possessed uniquely thin and blade-like teeth that were distinct among allosauroids.
A 2022 paper estimated the anterior bite force of Carcharodontosaurus saharicus at 11,312 newtons and the posterior bite force at 25,449 newtons.
A study by Donald Henderson suggests Carcharodontosaurus could physically lift animals weighing up to 424 kilograms with its jaws.
Fossilized tracks suggest Carcharodontosaurus could run at speeds of 8.5 m/s (around 30 km/h), though this estimate is now controversial.
The genus was first described in 1925 by Charles Depéret and Justin Savornin based on two lost fossil teeth found in Algeria.
French paleontologist René Lavocat first suggested the presence of Carcharodontosaurus in the Lower Douira Formation in 1954 based on fragmentary fossils.
In 2025, the main specimen was redescribed as the holotype of a distinct genus named Tameryraptor.
The subfamily Carcharodontosaurinae, containing Carcharodontosaurus, was likely restricted to the southern continent of Gondwana, where it probably served as an apex predator.
Carcharodontosaurus had a high tooth replacement rate, allowing damaged teeth to be replaced easily, unlike extant bone-crushing mammals.
The lower bite force of Carcharodontosaurus compared to Tyrannosaurus implies that it likely did not eat bones.
Isotopic analyses suggest Carcharodontosaurus was more terrestrial than the contemporary Spinosaurus, which pursued semi-aquatic habits.
The neotype skull of Carcharodontosaurus saharicus preserves pathologies including signs of biting, infection, and breaks.
A later study identified an unusual bony projection on the nasal of Carcharodontosaurus saharicus as a potential bite mark.
Daniel Chure suggested that the bony shelf above Carcharodontosaurus's orbit was used for head-butting fights.
The brain of C. saharicus would generally have been similar to that of the related dinosaur Allosaurus fragilis.
Larsson found that the ratio of brain to total encephalon volume in Carcharodontosaurus was typical of a non-avian reptile.
Carcharodontosaurus is the type genus of the family Carcharodontosauridae and the subfamily Carcharodontosaurinae.
The clade Carcharodontosauridae was originally created by Stromer for Carcharodontosaurus and Bahariasaurus, but the name was not used until the late 20th century.
Carcharodontosaurus is more closely related to Tyrannotitan than to Giganotosaurus and Mapusaurus.
Carcharodontosaurus lived in Northwest Africa between 100 and 94 million years ago during the Cenomanian stage of the Late Cretaceous.
The type skull was found in Cenomanian-aged rocks of the Lower Douira Formation in Errachidia, southeastern Morocco.
Carcharodontosaurians have been found from the Late Jurassic to the Mid-Cretaceous on every continent except Antarctica.

This group of large predatory dinosaurs was one of the greatest hunters of the Mesozoic, dominating southern continents from the Albian to the Cenomanian before being replaced by abelisaurids at the end of the Cretaceous.
Many fossils from French expeditions in North Africa were assigned to Carcharodontosaurus based on limited information, though many now belong to other genera.
A 2016 study suggested that non-holotypic material assigned to C. iguidensis actually belongs to Sigilmassasaurus and an unrelated taxon, limiting the species to its holotype.
The Spanish tooth assigned to Carcharodontosaurus lacks typical carcharodontosaurid traits and resembles other allosauroids instead.
